extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and editors/commentators of classical geometry (Euclid)
extracted.subtask_description: Notes and editorial guidance for correctly formulating and proving propositions in Euclid's Elements (chiefly Books XI–XII). Emphasizes missing hypotheses, cases, uniqueness of constructions, and which steps must be demonstrated rather than assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume facts that require proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements such as 'a straight line cannot meet a straight line in more than one point' or that certain solids/angles are equal are sometimes left in the text as assumed; these are things to be demonstrated, not merely asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever a geometrical fact is used that is not an immediate definition or axiom, provide a demonstration. The notes point out several places (e.g., prop. 1 of Book XI, prop. 25/26) where claims have been assumed and ought to be proved or supplied with auxiliary propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove plane-incidence of connecting segments
rubrics_metrics.description: When two points are given in the same plane, the straight line joining them must be shown to lie in that plane rather than assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several propositions require the explicit statement or proof that the line joining two points in a plane is itself in that plane; include that hypothesis or prove it when invoking results that depend on it (see commentary on early props of Book XI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate and handle all cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions that admit multiple distinct cases (e.g. parallelograms that share a side, are separate, or partially overlap; insisting lines at right angles or not) should list and prove each case separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not collapse distinct geometric configurations into one undifferentiated argument. The notes flag several propositions (e.g. Props. XXIX, XXXI) where the Greek editor omitted cases or merged demonstrations; restore and treat cases explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure constructions determine a unique object
rubrics_metrics.description: When instructing to 'complete the solid' with a given base and altitude, the construction must uniquely define which solid is meant; otherwise the instruction is ambiguous because innumerable solids may share the same base and altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add further specification (for instance, name an insisting straight line such as 'one of its insisting straight lines is FD') so the constructed solid is uniquely determined (see note on Prop. XXXII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not deduce equality of solids from equal/similar faces without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not generally true that two solids are equal merely because they are contained by the same number of equal and similar plane faces; such equalities were sometimes assumed in earlier texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit demonstrations or add corrective propositions (the notes add propositions A, B, C) to justify claims about equality of solids; do not rely on an unproved 10th definition to stand in for a demonstration (see discussion of Props. XXV–XXVI and surrounding commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume equality of solid angles from equal plane angles
rubrics_metrics.description: The equality of two solid angles contained by the same number of equal plane angles is not generally self-evident and must be demonstrated (it holds automatically only in certain restricted cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming two solid angles are equal because their bounding plane angles are pairwise equal, supply a proof or limit the claim to the provable cases (e.g., the special case of three plane angles leads to spherical-triangle-like arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise about 'in the same plane' when citing prior props/defs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some earlier books/propositions tacitly assume 'in the same plane'; later uses must explicitly include 'in the same plane' where it is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you cite a proposition whose hypotheses include 'in the same plane' (or where that clause is needed), ensure that clause appears in the reference or in the current proposition's assumptions (see notes on Prop. XVI, and repeated observations throughout Book XI commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct corrupted or superfluous editorial insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many editions contain words or clauses that are corruptions or later insertions (repeated phrases, irrelevant clauses, wrong references) which distort the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and remove or correct such insertions (examples cited throughout: omitted phrases that should be proved, wrong references to other editions, and textual corruptions in Props. VIII, XV, XXXIV, etc.). Prefer the reading that restores logical coherence and minimal redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When relying on earlier axioms, verify applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing an axiom from an earlier book is legitimate only if that axiom actually provides the needed implication; do not substitute an axiom where a true demonstration is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes criticize substituting Barrow's or other editors' axioms to avoid proofs. If the axiom does not in fact yield the desired conclusion without extra premises, supply the missing proof rather than hiding it behind an axiom reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove that common sections or intersections are straight lines when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an argument depends on a plane intersection being a straight line (e.g., the common section of two planes), that fact must be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on readers to accept that an intersection is straight; either cite a proven proposition that establishes it, or include a direct demonstration (see Prop. III, VIII notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary repetition of well-established conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a conclusion has been proved many times earlier in the text, it may be redundant to restate it fully in every subsequent proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamline proofs by omitting needless repetition, but do so only when the omitted material truly adds no new needed content (see reasoning about omitted triangle equality in Prop. IV and related notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: When introducing new constructions, state all necessary auxiliary choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructions that depend on auxiliary choices (e.g., selection of a point, side, or line) must state those choices explicitly so the construction is reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Prop. XXXII the editor must require applying a parallelogram in a specified angle equal to some angle; likewise, always name picked points/lines that determine the figure uniquely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat ratio properties rigorously; don’t assume higher-power analogues without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties about duplicate or triplicate ratios (e.g., that triplicate ratios preserve equality relations) should be demonstrated, not assumed by analogy with the duplicate case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit demonstrations for ratio exponentiation properties (note on Prop. XXXVII: Euclid proved the duplicate-ratio case; the triplicate-case needs similar care).

rubrics_metrics.name: When adding corollaries or remarks, ensure their premises are proved earlier
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollaries that depend on prior propositions must only be stated when the prior proposition actually supplies the necessary premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes indicate places where a corollary was used to justify something while the necessary antecedent had not been proved (example: reliance on cor. of prop. 1, book 1). Check dependencies and supply missing proofs where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concise constructions when they are equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: If a simpler construction accomplishes the same goal (e.g., drawing a perpendicular to a plane by dropping a perpendicular to the planes' common section), prefer it and avoid introducing superfluous propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prop. XXXVIII note: drawing the perpendicular via the common section is shorter and clearer; avoid adding a separate proposition that does nothing new or useful for the book's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using the phrase 'in the same manner' check that the omitted demonstration is indeed identical or unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors sometimes write 'in the same manner' to avoid repetition, but this is only justified when the omitted part is truly the same or trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the omitted subcase requires distinct reasoning, include it; the notes flag spots where 'in the same manner' was used but a demonstration should have been kept or adjusted (see Prop. XX and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly prove planarity claims about bisectors/intersecting lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that certain bisectors or lines in opposite planes lie in one plane must be demonstrated rather than assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prop. XXXIX note: when a proof invokes that bisecting lines of opposite faces are coplanar, include a specific argument establishing that fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using definitions as axioms (and vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and axioms have different logical roles; turning what should be an axiom into a 'definition' (or the reverse) is improper and hides required justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criticism of Tacquet's 'definition' of equal solid angles (making an axiom-like claim a definition) illustrates that such moves are logically inappropriate. Keep axioms as axioms and provide proofs for definitional claims when they function as axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: When restoring or editing classical texts, prefer readings that preserve demonstrability and avoid gratuitous assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should correct the text to remove unwarranted assumptions, reinstate necessary hypotheses, and supply missing demonstrations rather than smoothing logic by adding unjustified clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the notes the editor distinguishes between genuine Euclid material and later corruptions; the guiding principle is to restore logical completeness (e.g., supply missing demonstrations for Props. 25–26, add propositions where necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: When deducing consequences about solids, ensure planar/spherical analogues are handled correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies between rectilineal and spherical geometry (e.g., equilateral implying equiangular) must be justified by appropriate theorems; one cannot simply transfer planar results without proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes indicate that demonstrating equal-sided spherical triangles are equiangular was necessary (Menelaus), and similar care is required when moving between flat and spherical/solid contexts.
